title: Awake Intubation (ICU)
sources: Critical Vector — Awake Intubation in the ICU (verified vs primary literature)
Russotto V et al. INTUBE study. JAMA 2021 (45.2% major peri-intubation adverse event)
Difficult Airway Society — topical local anaesthetic ceiling 9 mg/kg lean body weight
Propensity-matched ICU awake vs VL vs DL study (adverse events 2.2% vs 22% vs 47%)

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV awake-intubation guide. Who stays awake, when not to, topicalisation ceiling, 'just enough' sedation, the 7-step recipe, and DSI as the fallback.

purpose: Keep the sickest patients breathing through the intubation. Awake intubation preserves spontaneous ventilation, sympathetic tone, and airway reflexes — it buys time instead of racing a desaturation clock. The tube goes in BEFORE the patient goes to sleep.

nodes.prompt: 1. Decide — is this patient too sick for RSI?
nodes.body: RSI does three things at once: removes sympathetic tone (induction), eliminates spontaneous ventilation (paralytic), and switches to positive pressure (drops preload). Stay awake when the patient can't absorb even one: predicted difficult airway + difficult rescue; severe hypoxaemia (can't tolerate apnoea); shock / haemodynamic instability (can't tolerate induction); severe metabolic acidosis (compensatory tachypnoea is keeping them alive); right heart failure (positive pressure is a disaster). See the Physiologically Difficult Airway reference.

Uncooperative / combative patient who can't tolerate topicalisation → use DSI instead. True crash airway or cardiac arrest → no time, secure it now. Active vomiting / massive haematemesis → need paralysis + suction speed, not slow topicalisation. Local-anaesthetic allergy → no topicalisation, no awake intubation. Operator inexperience without backup → a poorly done awake intubation is worse than a well-executed RSI.

Glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg IV to dry secretions (lets lidocaine stick instead of washing off). Suction on. Backup plan verbalised (SGA, surgical airway kit open). Flexible bronchoscope or a hyperangulated-blade videolaryngoscope — VL is a legitimate alternative, not a downgrade; the best device is the one in skilled hands.

nodes.prompt: 3. Topicalise — this is where it succeeds or fails
nodes.body: Atomiser: 4% lidocaine to the oropharynx and hypopharynx. Nebuliser: 4% lidocaine 4–5 mL over 10–15 min if time allows. Spray-as-you-go: lidocaine through the scope's working channel onto the cords. Ceiling: 9 mg/kg LEAN body weight for topical airway use (DAS) — mucosal absorption is incomplete so plasma levels stay well below toxic at this dose.

nodes.prompt: 4. Sedate — 'just enough': calm, cooperative, spontaneously breathing (NOT asleep)
nodes.body: Dexmedetomidine — anxiolysis, antisialagogue, minimal respiratory depression; less hypoxaemia than remifentanil (RR 2.47). Load 1 mcg/kg over 10 min, then 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/hr; watch for bradycardia. Alternatives: remifentanil (great cough suppression, watch for apnoea + chest-wall rigidity), ketamine (dissociation with preserved reflexes, useful in the combative patient). If the patient stops breathing you've turned this into an RSI — with a mouth full of lidocaine and no paralytic on board.
High-flow nasal cannula at 40–60 L/min throughout the procedure.
Scope or VL. Confirm placement with waveform capnography (see the Capnography reference).
Give induction / sedation only AFTER the tube is confirmed. The tube goes in before the patient goes to sleep.

For the agitated / intolerant patient who can't cooperate with topicalisation: a dissociative dose of ketamine (~0.3 mg/kg reported for the apnoea-free window) to allow effective preoxygenation, then proceed. DSI is a preoxygenation strategy, not a separate induction technique.

checklist: Decision documented: physiologically or anatomically too high-risk for RSI
No contraindication to an awake approach (cooperative, not crashing, no LA allergy, operator competent + backup present)
Glycopyrrolate given; suction, SGA, and surgical airway kit at the bedside
Topical lidocaine total kept ≤ 9 mg/kg lean body weight
Sedation titrated to calm-and-breathing, not asleep
Tube confirmed with waveform capnography BEFORE induction
